description: A learned name inside a Hindi sentence written in Latin script. Kivi is built for Indian users and Saaras emits code-mixed output, so this is ordinary input, not an edge case.
asr: kal aditya ke saath meeting hai
formatted: Kal Aditya ke saath meeting hai.
expected: Kal Aaditya ke saath meeting hai.
rationale: Matching is on phonetic skeletons of Latin tokens, so the surrounding language is irrelevant. Nothing in the design is English-specific.

description: An unobserved spelling inside a Hinglish sentence, with a second identity in the same clause.
asr: adithya ko bol do ki kiwi build ready hai
formatted: Adithya ko bol do ki Kiwi build ready hai.
expected: Aaditya ko bol do ki Kivi build ready hai.
rationale: 'build' is a Kivi context term and survives being embedded in Hindi, because context terms are matched as skeletons rather than as English words.

description: Two product identities in a Hinglish sentence, both misheard.
asr: mujhe sarwam ka kiwi service check karna hai
formatted: Mujhe Sarwam ka Kiwi service check karna hai.
expected: Mujhe Sarvam ka Kivi service check karna hai.
rationale: Sarvam and service both support the product reading of Kiwi even though the carrier language is Hindi.

description: Two people, each reached by a different retrieval tier, in one Hindi sentence.
asr: aaj chinmoy aur vakaria dono aaye the
formatted: Aaj Chinmoy aur Vakaria dono aaye the.
expected: Aaj Chinmay aur Vekariya dono aaye the.
rationale: Chinmoy resolves on the loose consonant key and Vakaria on the loose key too; both work unchanged inside Hindi.

description: Hindi possessive particle rather than an English clitic.
asr: adhitya ka branch merge kar do
formatted: Adhitya ka branch merge kar do.
expected: Aaditya ka branch merge kar do.
rationale: Possession is a separate word in Hindi, so no suffix handling is needed; the span is a bare token.

description: THE TRAP, IN HINGLISH. 'I am eating a kiwi.' The homophone guard must hold when the carrier language is not English.
rationale: No Kivi context term appears. The guard depends on positive contextual evidence rather than on recognising English food words, so it does not degrade in Hindi.
'bazaar' and 'aana' belong to no memory. Nothing supports the product reading.

description: An unknown person in a Hindi sentence.
asr: rahul ko bol do ki main aa raha hoon
formatted: Rahul ko bol do ki main aa raha hoon.
expected: Rahul ko bol do ki main aa raha hoon.
rationale: Memory must stay out of the way regardless of carrier language.

description: Cross-script memory: the same person, written in Devanagari, never taught in that script.
rationale: Authored when Devanagari produced no phonetic keys at all, expecting no intervention. Transliteration into the skeleton alphabet closed that: आदित्य romanises to 'aaditya' and skeletonises to 'aditia', the same key the Latin correction produced. The user taught this word once, in one script, and gets it back in both. The canonical form is written as the user taught it, which is a deliberate choice and an arguable one for a person's name in Hindi prose.

description: Cross-script CONTEXT, as opposed to cross-script identity.
rationale: Authored as a known-hard failure, and it failed for two commits. 'कीवी' is a homophone of the fruit so the guard demands supporting context, and the support here is 'सर्विस' -- the English word 'service' borrowed into Hindi. Two bugs kept them apart. English 'service' skeletonised to 'servike', because every bare c was mapped to k rather than only the hard ones; and context was matched on strict skeletons only, so 'servise' and 'sarvis' still never met. Fixing the soft c and indexing context under the loose consonant key as well closed both, with no measured cost: 0 false positives across 1,626 adversarial sentences either side of the change.

description: Both behaviours in a single sentence: a Devanagari person resolves, a Devanagari homophone does not.
asr: the कीवी was sour but the meeting with आदित्य went well
formatted: The कीवी was sour but the meeting with आदित्य went well.
expected: The कीवी was sour but the meeting with Aaditya went well.
rationale: The sharpest single test of cross-script behaviour, because the two spans need opposite answers. आदित्य is an unambiguous person and resolves on the strict key. कीवी is a homophone of the fruit, and with 'sour' rather than any Kivi context term present the guard holds -- in a script the guard was originally blind to. Getting one right and the other wrong would be worse than getting both wrong.
